issues.legal_issue: Courts do not re-examine the merits of a considered policy decision to undertake an infrastructure project unless the decision-making process is unlawful, arbitrary, irrational, or transgresses fundamental rights.
material_facts: The project had been considered at several stages by the Government and expert bodies, and the Government had adopted a system for its execution.
The challenge sought, among other things, to halt a project that was already at an advanced stage.
issues.conclusion: The Court would not revisit the policy choice to construct the dam or substitute its assessment for the Government’s, while retaining the duty to ensure that the law is followed and fundamental rights are not impermissibly infringed.
issues.legal_principle: Applying Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India, (2000) 10 SCC 664, and drawing an analogy with BALCO Employees’ Union (Regd.) v. Union of India, (2002) 2 SCC 333, the Court treated the conception and decision to undertake an infrastructure project as policy matters. Judicial review remains available for illegality, infringement of fundamental rights, arbitrariness, irrationality, or failure to consider relevant material.

rule.if: infrastructure_policy_case and considered_policy_decision and (expert_review_completed or implementation_system_put_in_place) and not (arbitrary_decision or irrational_decision or legal_violation or impermissible_fundamental_rights_infringement)

predicates.infrastructure_policy_case: The proceeding challenges a governmental decision to undertake or execute an infrastructure project.
predicates.considered_policy_decision: The government made the project decision after considering the relevant policy choices.
predicates.expert_review_completed: One or more expert bodies examined the project or its relevant effects.
predicates.implementation_system_put_in_place: The government established a system for carrying out the project decision.
predicates.legal_violation: The challenged decision or its implementation violated the law.
predicates.impermissible_fundamental_rights_infring: The project decision impermissibly transgressed a fundamental right.

issues.definition: When a project decision was considered and reviewed and is not shown to be unlawful, arbitrary, irrational, or an impermissible infringement of fundamental rights, courts do not substitute their view for the government’s policy choice.

issues.legal_issue: A court does not compel additional technical safety tests when the government has made a well-informed decision based on expert consideration and the proposed tests are additional precautions rather than evidence of an unsafe design.
material_facts: The dam’s seismic safety was examined by multiple technical bodies and experts, including a group of five experts appointed during the proceedings.
The group unanimously concluded that the design was expected to be structurally safe against the maximum credible earthquake during the system’s economic performance life.
Four experts suggested additional three-dimensional non-linear analysis and simulated dam-break analysis as abundant caution, while one did not consider them necessary.
The Government considered the further recommendations with technical bodies and decided not to require the additional studies.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to re-examine the dam’s safety or direct the additional tests, finding no basis to interfere with the Government’s decision.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied administrative-law review focused on the decision-making process rather than the merits of technical judgments. It relied on Tehri Bandh Virodhi Sangarsh Samiti v. State of U.P., 1992 Supp (1) SCC 44, which had previously declined to interfere after the Government considered expert safety opinions, and distinguished A.P. Pollution Control Board v. Prof. M.V. Nayudu (Retd.), (1999) 2 SCC 718, because the experts here did not disagree that the dam was safe and the additional studies were recommended only as abundant caution.

rule.if: constitutional_public_interest_petition and dam_safety_challenge and expert_consensus_design_safe and additional_tests_recommended_only_as_precaution and government_considered_expert_views and not (bad_faith or arbitrary_decision or irrational_decision)

predicates.constitutional_public_interest_petition: The proceeding is a constitutional public-interest challenge to a project.
predicates.dam_safety_challenge: The challengers allege that the project structure is unsafe.
predicates.expert_consensus_design_safe: The experts who assessed the design agreed that it was safe under the assessed conditions.
predicates.additional_tests_recommended_only_as_pre: Some experts proposed further testing as an additional precaution rather than finding the design unsafe.
predicates.government_considered_expert_views: The government considered the expert opinions before deciding whether to require further testing.
predicates.bad_faith: The government made the testing decision in bad faith.
predicates.arbitrary_decision: The government’s testing decision was arbitrary.
predicates.irrational_decision: The government’s testing decision was irrational.

issues.definition: Where experts agree that a structure is safe, proposed further tests are only precautionary, and the government has considered the expert views without bad faith or irrationality, a court does not compel those tests.

issues.legal_issue: The precautionary principle does not automatically shift the burden of proof to the proponent of a project when the project is not a polluting industry and its environmental effects are known and capable of mitigation.
material_facts: The project was the construction of a large dam, not a nuclear establishment or polluting industry.
The Court considered the effects of dam construction on the environment to be known and considered that mitigative steps could be taken.
The project had environmental clearance subject to specified safeguards and action plans.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the precautionary principle, as applied to uncertain pollution risks, did not require the Court to presume ecological disaster or to re-examine the project on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the explanation in Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India, (2000) 10 SCC 664, distinguishing the approach in A.P. Pollution Control Board v. Prof. M.V. Nayudu (Retd.), (1999) 2 SCC 718. It treated the precautionary burden as ordinarily applicable where the extent of likely damage is unknown, and sustainable development as applicable where the project’s effects are known and mitigation can preserve ecological balance.

rule.if: environmental_public_interest_case and large_dam_project and project_effects_known and mitigative_measures_available and not polluting_industry

predicates.environmental_public_interest_case: The proceeding raises a public-interest challenge concerning a project’s environmental effects.
predicates.large_dam_project: The challenged project is the construction of a large dam.
predicates.project_effects_known: The environmental effects of the project are known rather than materially uncertain.
predicates.mitigative_measures_available: Measures are available to address or mitigate the project’s environmental effects.
predicates.polluting_industry: The challenged project is a polluting industry.

issues.definition: When a public-interest case concerns a large dam whose environmental effects are known and can be mitigated, the precautionary burden shift used for uncertain pollution risks is not required.

issues.legal_issue: Sustainable development requires strict compliance with environmental-clearance conditions, including conditions requiring environmental safeguards to progress alongside engineering works.
material_facts: Environmental clearance was granted subject to studies, action plans, and safeguards being implemented pari passu with the engineering works.
The conditions covered environmental measures including catchment treatment, command area development, flora and fauna, water quality, and related safeguards.

The record disclosed delays and lapses in some measures, but the Government filed status information indicating substantial compliance and stated that impoundment would not begin until the clearance conditions were fulfilled.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the clearance conditions had to be strictly complied with and accepted the Government’s assurance that impoundment would not be allowed until the conditions were fulfilled; it transferred the proceedings for continued monitoring.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that sustainable development is integral to the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution and is necessary to balance environmental protection with development. It relied on the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, and on Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India, (1996) 5 SCC 647; M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, (2002) 4 SCC 356; State of Himachal Pradesh v. Ganesh Wood Products, (1995) 6 SCC 363; and M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath, (1997) 1 SCC 388. The power to impose conditions under the Act is coupled with a duty to ensure compliance.

predicates.infrastructure_project_with_conditional_: The project is an infrastructure project that received environmental clearance subject to conditions.
predicates.clearance_conditions_require_parallel_im: The clearance requires environmental studies, plans, or safeguards to progress alongside engineering work.
predicates.environmental_safeguards_remain_to_be_co: One or more required environmental safeguards remain incomplete.

issues.definition: If a project’s environmental clearance requires safeguards to progress with construction and any safeguards remain incomplete, impoundment must wait until the clearance conditions are fulfilled.

issues.legal_issue: Courts should not reassess the substantive choices in a rehabilitation package adopted after expert deliberation and consideration of local conditions, but affected people must be rehabilitated before submergence.
material_facts: An expert committee examined rehabilitation and the Government adopted a package addressing affected families, including families affected by the associated dam and reservoir rim.
The petitioners challenged aspects of the package, including land allocation and the treatment of separate family units.
The Court considered land scarcity and the conditions of the hilly region, and found that the package had been formulated after deliberation.
The Court stated that rehabilitation must precede submergence and that there could be no impoundment before rehabilitation was completed.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the challenged policy choices in the rehabilitation package, but required eligible affected people to be rehabilitated before impoundment, with rehabilitation taking place before submergence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Article 21 and the rehabilitation principles recognized in Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India, (2000) 10 SCC 664, and B.D. Sharma v. Union of India, 1992 Supp (3) SCC 93. It treated rehabilitation as a logical corollary of Article 21 and held that the package’s policy choices were not for judicial substitution where they had been deliberated upon with relevant conditions in view.

rule.if: dam_displacement_case and rehabilitation_package_adopted_after_deliberation and local_conditions_considered and affected_people_require_relocation

predicates.dam_displacement_case: The proceeding concerns displacement caused by a dam or comparable project.
predicates.rehabilitation_package_adopted_after_del: The government adopted a rehabilitation package after considering expert recommendations or other relevant material.
predicates.local_conditions_considered: The package was formulated with relevant local conditions, including the availability of land, in view.
predicates.affected_people_require_relocation: People affected by the project must be relocated.

issues.definition: In a dam-displacement case, courts defer to a deliberated package that considers local conditions but require affected people to be rehabilitated before impoundment.

issues.legal_issue: A constitutional public-interest environmental proceeding may be transferred to a High Court for effective local monitoring and enforcement while preserving issues already decided by the Supreme Court.
material_facts: The proceeding was brought under Article 32 and raised continuing environmental-compliance and rehabilitation concerns concerning a project located within a State.
The Supreme Court found that local conditions and the implementation of environmental safeguards could be more effectively monitored by the High Court.
The Supreme Court had already decided the project’s safety and other specified issues and directed that they not be re-examined.
issues.conclusion: The Court transferred the proceedings to the High Court to be dealt with as if filed there, leaving it free to pass appropriate orders on continuing matters but not to re-examine issues already decided.
issues.legal_principle: Applying Article 32 and relying on Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India, (1996) 5 SCC 281; M.L. Sud v. Union of India, 1992 Supp (2) SCC 123; and Mohan Chand v. Union of India, 1995 Supp (3) SCC 425, the Court held that Article 32 proceedings may be transferred in appropriate cases so that local facts and enforcement can be addressed effectively.

rule.if: article_32_environmental_proceeding and continuing_local_compliance_issues and high_court_better_placed_to_monitor and issues_already_decided_by_supreme_court

predicates.article_32_environmental_proceeding: The matter is an environmental public-interest proceeding brought directly before the Supreme Court under its constitutional writ jurisdiction.
predicates.continuing_local_compliance_issues: The matter requires continued monitoring of compliance or implementation in a particular region.
predicates.high_court_better_placed_to_monitor: The High Court is better positioned to assess local conditions and monitor implementation.
predicates.issues_already_decided_by_supreme_court: The Supreme Court has already decided some issues in the proceeding.

issues.definition: When a constitutional environmental proceeding requires continuing local monitoring, it may be transferred to a better-positioned High Court, which must leave issues already decided by the Supreme Court undisturbed.

issues.legal_issue: In dissent, additional seismic-safety analyses, independent monitoring of clearance conditions, and completed rehabilitation were required before further impoundment.
material_facts: The dam was located in a seismically unstable region and four of five safety experts recommended additional three-dimensional non-linear analysis and simulated dam-break analysis as abundant caution.
The dissent considered that environmental-clearance conditions had not been adequately monitored and that rehabilitation remained incomplete.
The clearance required environmental conditions to be implemented pari passu with engineering work.
issues.conclusion: The dissent would have prohibited closing the diversion tunnels for impoundment until the additional safety analyses were completed and assessed, required an expert committee to report regularly on compliance and rehabilitation, and prohibited impoundment until rehabilitation was complete.
issues.legal_principle: The dissent relied on the precautionary principle in the Rio Declaration, treating it as part of domestic law through the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. It relied on sections 3 and 5 of that Act, Rule 5 of the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986, the environmental impact assessment notification of 1994, M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, (1997) 2 SCC 353, and Karjan Jalasay Yojana Assargrasth Shakhar Ane Snagharsh Samiti v. State of Gujarat, AIR 1987 SC 532, as well as the principle that rehabilitation must protect the livelihood and dignity of displaced people.

predicates.dam_safety_and_environmental_clearance_c: The proceeding challenges the safety of a dam and compliance with its environmental clearance.
predicates.experts_recommend_additional_safety_anal: One or more experts recommend further safety analysis before impoundment.
predicates.clearance_conditions_not_fully_complied_: Environmental-clearance conditions have not yet been fully complied with.
predicates.rehabilitation_incomplete: Some people entitled to rehabilitation have not yet been rehabilitated.

issues.definition: Under the dissent’s approach, if further expert safety analysis is recommended or clearance conditions remain unfulfilled and rehabilitation is incomplete, impoundment must not proceed until safety review and rehabilitation are complete.
